name: Omar Olsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, political parties or government. We don't sell anything or campaign. Your answers are confidential, so you can give me the public version and your private view. What does a normal working day look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm 27, a senior developer at a tech company that makes software for warehouse dispatch teams. I start by reading the overnight error log, then lead a small team through fixes and new features. I use an AI coding tool every day, but the useful part of my job is finding out why a shipment went to the wrong loading bay. I have a master's degree and still like getting a messy system to behave.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What does the job mean for your life outside the office?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The title came early, but the pay is low for senior software work. I share a rental flat with my partner, whose café shifts change week to week, and we have less than a month of expenses saved. There are few developer jobs nearby, so I'd likely search remotely if this company cut back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the team to keep using the coding assistant for tests and dull formatting. It saves me an hour here and there, which is worth having. I wouldn't claim it can understand a warehouse at shift change without us checking it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The plateau would leave me with a job I enjoy, but not with much cash. Our rent went up this year and my partner's café shifts can disappear for a week. The emergency is already in the bank balance, not in the forecast for AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep building and checking the dispatch software, using the assistant where it already helps. This payday I'd start a small automatic transfer to a savings account and set a target of one month's rent. During the first year, I'd ask for a salary review with the error fixes I've delivered written down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, even though the job itself would keep its shape. I like the work and I'd welcome a little less drudgery. My partner's café shifts swing, and one missed pay cheque could force us to ask for help with rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which fix would you bring to the pay review?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd bring the loading-bay error we cut from twelve cases a week to three. The warehouse lead notices that more than lines of code. A number makes the salary talk less like pleading.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens if the savings transfer is too much one month?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd lower it for that month, then put it back when my partner gets more shifts. I won't let a tidy savings plan bounce the rent payment. We can review the account together each payday.

say: I'd keep using the **coding assistant** for tests and formatting while checking warehouse decisions myself.
I'd say the tool saves some **time**, with no radical change to our dispatch work.
think: I know a **rent rise** and my partner's uneven café shifts already strain our household.
I have less than **one month saved**, leaving us exposed even if AI changes little.
do: Keep building and **checking dispatch software** while using the existing assistant on routine work.
Transfer a small sum each payday toward **one month's rent** and request a salary review with measured fixes.
feel: **Anxious** about uneven household income and rent, despite modest time savings at work.
S0.quote: The emergency is already in the bank balance, not in the forecast for AI.
fieldNote: He uses AI **every day** already, but still judges its output against warehouse operations.
His underlying worry is **household cash**, shaped by rent and variable café shifts.
The salary request rests on a **measured error reduction**, which fits his practical approach.

steps.text: Keep checking dispatch software while using the coding assistant for tests
Transfer a small amount each payday toward one month of rent

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell colleagues we should use these tools to clear the backlog and measure the mistakes. I would offer to run a trial on our list of shipments that need a person to fix a problem. More output sounds good, but we should ask whether management means to stop replacing people who leave.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my own job could shrink once the tool handles code, checks and customer messages together. I might become the person who chooses the exceptions, but that's fewer hours than our whole team works now. I'm quicker to try the tools than most people here, and that doesn't make my salary safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week I'd propose a four-week trial using real exception cases with a person signing off each change. I'd document what the tool misses and learn the new workflow well enough to run it. If the company cuts hours in the first year, I'd update my remote-job portfolio and cut our restaurant spending until income steadies.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, with some energy in it. I want to be the person who understands the new system, and I know that won't guarantee a full-time post. I feel the household budget underneath every clever demo.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would count as a failed trial?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the tool sends a shipment to the wrong bay twice in a month, the warehouse team loses trust. I'd count those errors, not just minutes saved. Our customer pays for freight that arrives, not for neat code.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you tell your team your hours may be at risk?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, once I have a real figure from management rather than a guess. I'd say the trial could mean fewer hours and ask them to keep examples of the work humans still catch. I wouldn't sell it as a guarantee of safety.

say: I'd offer a **four-week trial** on shipment exceptions, with people checking every change.
I'd ask whether faster work means **unfilled vacancies** on our team.
think: I worry AI could combine **coding, checking and replies**, leaving fewer paid hours for my team.
I know being an **early user** of the tools would not guarantee my salary.
do: Run a **four-week exception trial** and count wrong-bay errors.
Learn the **new workflow** well enough to run it and document what AI misses.
Update my **remote-job portfolio** and cut restaurant meals if hours fall during the first year.
feel: **Anxious** about household income, alongside interest in building the new workflow.
S1.quote: I feel the household budget underneath every clever demo.
fieldNote: He volunteers to **trial AI** but wants errors counted alongside time saved.
The chance to lead a new workflow gives him **agency**, while fewer paid hours remain plausible.
Remote applications and cheaper meals are **conditional** on a cut in hours.

steps.text: Run a four-week AI trial on shipment exceptions and count wrong-bay errors
Cut restaurant meals if developer hours fall
Update a portfolio for remote developer jobs if hours fall

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the company to stop calling developer jobs safe just because warehouses still need people. Full thinking AI by 2028 could write our software and handle many exceptions before robots reach loading bays around 2031. I'd ask for a plan for the people who currently build the system.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect the value of my code to fall quickly, and this company could cut most of the team. I'm good at the work and already use AI daily, but a cheaper system doing nearly all thinking work changes the arithmetic. With under a month's savings, I don't have time to wait for a perfect new career.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now I'd ask the warehouse lead to let me shadow one dispatch shift a week and ask management what work remains paid. I'd save every spare amount and build a list of nearby operations roles with their wages. In the first year after 2028, if the developer role ends, I'd take paid dispatch or systems support work while applying for any income help we qualify for; I wouldn't wait until the 2031 robots arrive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. My mind starts drawing diagrams of what we could build, and then I remember the rent date. I can move fast, but two years isn't much runway with less than a month of expenses saved and rent due.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask the warehouse lead on the first shift?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask which problem still needs someone standing at the loading bay when the computer says the shipment is ready. I'd follow one wrong-label case from scan to truck. I want to know what a support job actually pays for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you explain the risk to your partner?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd show my partner the exact gap between rent and one possible dispatch wage. We should decide together what to cut before a layoff makes the choice for us. The café shifts can't be our rescue plan.

say: I'd say **thinking AI in 2028** reaches our software before warehouse robots arrive around 2031.
I'd ask management for a **staffing plan** for the people building the dispatch system.
think: I think most of our team's **coding value** could vanish quickly, despite my skill and daily AI use.
I have under **one month saved**, leaving little time to find a new paid role.
do: Shadow **one dispatch shift** weekly and ask which operations work still pays.
Save **every spare amount** and list nearby operations wages before 2028.
Take **paid dispatch support** and seek available income help if my developer role ends after AGI arrives.
feel: **Alarmed** by likely income loss and a rent deadline, though he can act quickly.
S2.quote: I can move fast, but two years isn't much runway with less than a month of expenses saved and rent due.
fieldNote: His daily AI use does not soften the **income threat** from full thinking AI.
He seeks **paid warehouse-adjacent work** before robots arrive, while acknowledging that option may later narrow.
Help and a dispatch job are **conditional** on losing the developer role.

steps.text: Shadow one warehouse dispatch shift weekly to learn support work
Put every spare amount into emergency savings before 2028
Take paid dispatch or systems support work if development ends
Apply for available income help if development ends

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell colleagues five years is enough to run real experiments rather than argue over demos. I'd propose a small tool for warehouse staff that we can test with users while we still have wages. Still, full thinking AI in 2031 means our software work changes before robots reach the bays around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I can build something useful with AI, but useful and paid aren't the same. The employer might own the customer relationships and use AGI to replace our code work. Five years lets me test whether a warehouse will actually pay for a better exception log, rather than gamble rent on a pitch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Next month I'd talk to three warehouse supervisors about lost shipments and mock up a simple log of shipment problems on evenings, testing a new AI coding workflow against three real shipment problems. I would keep my job and save two months of expenses before spending on any launch. In the first year after 2031, if at least two warehouses pay a monthly fee, I'd make the log a small side business; if not, I'd search paid operations software roles.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I can breathe. A trial with three real supervisors is something I can do while paid. I don't need to pretend every experiment will become a company.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make the side business real rather than a hobby?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two warehouses paying a monthly fee would be the minimum. I'd ask what they currently spend fixing mistakes and price below that. A compliment from a supervisor is not revenue.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You sound hopeful, but you still call yourself anxious. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because my partner's shifts and our rent don't wait for my product to find a buyer. I wouldn't quit a wage on the strength of a prototype. Hope doesn't cover the deposit on another flat.

say: I'd propose **real warehouse trials** while developers still have wages.
I'd point out that **2031 thinking AI** changes software work before 2034 robots reach loading bays.
think: I could build a useful **exception log**, but customers may not pay for it.
I think five years lets me test demand without **gambling rent** on a pitch.
do: Interview **three supervisors** and test a new AI coding workflow on their shipment problems next month.
Save **two months' expenses** before paying to launch anything.
Start a **paid side business** after 2031 only with two monthly subscribers; otherwise seek paid operations software work.
feel: **Anxious** about rent, with breathing room to test demand while earning wages.
S3.quote: A compliment from a supervisor is not revenue.
fieldNote: His appetite for new tools is checked by a **paying-customer test** and a savings floor.
He plans to keep the **developer wage** while testing an exception-log product.

steps.text: Test a new AI coding workflow on three supervisors’ shipment problems
Save two months of expenses before paying launch costs
Start a shipment-problem log business after 2031 only if two warehouses subscribe
Search paid operations software jobs if fewer than two warehouses subscribe after 2031

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell a new developer to learn the warehouse as thoroughly as the code. A decade gives us a chance to build tools with the staff who use them and see whether customers pay. It also gives firms a decade to replace our thinking work by 2036, so I wouldn't promise a permanent role.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could be in my late thirties with a savings cushion and a tested product by then. I might also discover that AI makes the product easy for anyone to copy. The extra time is useful because I can learn the market, not because I can outrun the technology forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd set a monthly savings transfer now and use one evening a week to sit with dispatch users before writing features. I'd only spend on the shipment-problem log after two warehouses agree to paid trials, and I'd keep my developer job until service revenue covers basic bills for several months. In the first year after 2036, if coding income falls, I'd grow the paid service only if it reaches that bill-covering level; otherwise I'd apply for warehouse systems operations jobs only where paid vacancies exist.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious under the calm talk. Ten years gives me time to test things and save, but our rent and my partner's changing shifts are problems now. I would still grieve losing the part of the job where I make a difficult fix myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if another firm copies the exception log?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask users which part of their shift still hurts and improve that, rather than borrowing money for an expensive feature race. If customers stop paying, I'd close the side project. I won't keep a side project alive with rent money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the later robot date change your plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Robots around 2039 might change loading-bay staffing, but our software work faces AGI in 2036. I'd keep checking whether operations jobs actually exist before calling them my fallback. A date on a card doesn't guarantee a vacancy.

say: I'd urge developers to learn **warehouse work** and test tools with paying users over the decade.
I'd avoid promising a **permanent coding role** once thinking AI arrives in 2036.
think: I think a decade could give me **savings and customers**, though AI might make my product easy to copy.
I value **market learning** over pretending I can outrun AI forever.
do: Make a **monthly savings transfer** while the developer wage lasts.
Seek **two paid trials** before product spending and keep my wage until service revenue covers bills for months.
Seek **paid warehouse systems vacancies** if coding income falls after 2036 and the service still cannot cover bills.
feel: **Anxious** about current rent and uneven shifts, despite ten years to test and save.
S4.quote: I won't keep a side project alive with rent money.
fieldNote: He uses the long horizon to require **paid trials** before spending on a product.
His plan keeps a **wage floor** until service revenue covers basic bills for several months.
He sees **2039 robots** as a later risk to operations work, not extra protection for coding.

steps.text: Transfer money monthly into savings while developer wages continue
Sell shipment-problem log trials to two warehouses and retain wages until revenue covers bills for months
Apply for paid warehouse systems vacancies if coding income falls and service revenue cannot cover bills

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most, even though I use AI all the time. The software work could shrink before I have a cushion or real customers for another idea. A notice period, paid time to learn dispatch operations, and temporary bill help if the job ends would make the difference.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask whether the warehouse workers get a say in the tools we build. I can make a clean screen from my desk and still make warehouse workers' night shift harder. I'd want them in the room before we call an AI change a success.

headlineQuote: I can make a clean screen from my desk and still make warehouse workers' night shift harder.
portrait: Omar is a **27-year-old senior developer** with a master's degree, making dispatch software and using AI daily.
His **low senior pay**, under one month saved, variable household shifts and few local developer jobs constrain his risks.
In **AI Plateau**, he keeps coding while building a rent buffer and seeking a salary review.
In **Steady Disruption**, he offers an AI trial but expects possible cuts to paid hours.
Fast AGI **alarms** him; longer timelines allow paid product trials, yet present rent and shift worries keep him anxious.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could shrink his software work before savings or paying customers give him another route.
whatWouldHelp: A **notice period**, paid dispatch training and temporary help with bills after job loss would help.
